The true size of the 1.96 rule runs from 1.4% to 3.9%. It never reaches 5%, and at 40 items split 20/20 it is still short by a factor of 1.27. Dichotomous items are the worst, with the polytomous-versus-dichotomous contrast at 0.0137, and a sample two logits off target is nearly as bad at 0.0177. Both findings match the RCI chapter (Section 7.5 and Section 7.6), where response categories moved the critical value mainly in the step from two to more than two, and where mistargeting dropped the pooled value from 1.695 to 1.522 because a floor-bound sample is located where the statistic is most damped.
The effective test length here is the subtest, not the scale, which is what makes the protocol worse than the change case rather than equivalent to it. The length table in Section 7.5 reads 1.644 at 4 items, 1.725 at 6, 1.815 at 10 and 1.868 at 20, four categories throughout and persons from \(N(0, 1.4)\). A 20-item scale splitting 10/10 is governed by two 10-item instruments. The published recommendation to use the protocol with at least 12 item response thresholds (Horton & Tennant, 2010; Tennant & Pallant, 2006) amounts to four items at four categories, which is the worst row of that table.

title: 4  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
section: 4.6 A large share of respondents cannot be flagged at all
text:
4.6 A large share of respondents cannot be flagged at all
The last column above counts respondents for whom no attainable pair of subtest scores produces \(|t| > 1.96\). Their contribution to the significant count is zero with probability one, not 0.05. At 20 dichotomous items that is 44% of the sample and on an off-target polytomous scale 46%.


Code
panel <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA) {
  g <- split_grid(mk(k, ncat), idxA)
  a <- alpha_by_r(cond_null(g, 0), 1.96)
  data.frame(label = label, r = seq_along(a) - 1L, alpha = a)
}
d_fig <- rbind(
  panel("20 items, 4 cat, 10/10", 20, 4, seq(1, 20, by = 2)),
  panel("12 items, 4 cat, 6/6",   12, 4, seq(1, 12, by = 2)),
  panel("20 items, 2 cat, 10/10", 20, 2, seq(1, 20, by = 2)))
d_fig$label <- factor(d_fig$label, levels = unique(d_fig$label))

ggplot(d_fig, aes(r, alpha)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_step(direction = "mid") +
  facet_wrap(~ label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Total score across all items", y = "Exact type I error of 1.96")








Figure 4.1: Exact size of the 1.96 rule by total score, under a perfectly unidimensional Rasch model. Weighted by a \(N(0, 1.4)\) latent density to give the sample means quoted in the text. The dashed line is the 5% the protocol assumes. Scores at both ends carry a size of zero because no attainable split of that total clears 1.96.





The sawtooth is discreteness. Adjacent total scores differ in how many attainable splits they have and where those splits fall relative to the cutoff, so the size of the test alternates rather than varying smoothly. The RCI chapter found the same structure in the conditional critical value, which formed an arch across the score range rather than a constant.
Figure 4.1 also shows that the conservatism is not a uniform shrinkage. Around the middle of the scale the size peaks at 0.062, 0.062 and 0.054 in the three panels, so the test is mildly anti-conservative there. Under the \(N(0, 1.4)\) weighting, 20%, 6% and 10% of respondents hold a total score whose size exceeds 0.05. The whole of the deficit comes from the ends, where attainable scores run out and the size falls to zero. Averaging over the score distribution is what the protocol does when it pools respondents into one proportion, and that average is what has to be compared with 5%, but a reader should know that the pooled figure is combining two opposite behaviours rather than describing a test that is uniformly too strict.

The RCI chapter (Section 7.4) corrected an earlier belief that two-sided simulated critical values were asymmetric: under the change null the two occasions are exchangeable, so the difference is symmetric about zero however skewed \(\hat\theta\) is, and exchangeability fails only when the occasions differ in missingness. Subtests break exchangeability by construction, because they differ in length, targeting and information. A balanced interleaved split is nearly symmetric, so the change result transfers there. An unbalanced or difficulty-confounded split is not. The ten easiest items against the ten hardest gives correct two-sided values of -2.001 and 1.578, so the upper value is stricter than 1.96 while the lower is more lenient. A principal component of residuals often separates items by location as well as by content, which makes that row the relevant one.
The last column is \(\max_r |E[\hat\theta_A - \hat\theta_B \mid r]|\) under a perfectly unidimensional model. On a 4/16 split it reaches 0.557 logits, purely from the difference in WLE bias between a four-item and a sixteen-item subtest. That is model-implied signal with no multidimensionality behind it. Reporting quantity and units at every surface, as the RCI chapter insists, matters here: the gap is in logits, the t is unitless, and only the second is being compared with 1.96.

text:
4.8 What happens at the count level


Code
count_null <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA, n, mu = 0, sigma = 1.4) {
  thr <- mk(k, ncat); g <- split_grid(thr, idxA); cn <- cond_null(g, 0)
  fr <- score_weights(thr, mu, sigma); fr <- fr / sum(fr)
  a  <- alpha_by_r(cn, 1.96)
  nr <- round(n * fr); p_i <- rep(a, times = nr)
  d  <- pois_binom(p_i); cnt <- seq_along(d) - 1L; m <- length(p_i)
  mean_p <- sum(d * cnt) / m
  data.frame(config = label, n = m,
             mean_p = 100 * mean_p,
             q95    = 100 * cnt[which(cumsum(d) >= 0.95)[1L]] / m,
             p_over = sum(d[cnt / m > 0.05]),
             sd_pb  = sqrt(sum(d * cnt^2) - sum(d * cnt)^2),
             sd_bin = sqrt(m * mean_p * (1 - mean_p)),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

At \(n = 1000\), observing more than 5% significant tests is an event of probability 0.0007, 0.0000, 0.0000 and 0.044 under a perfectly unidimensional model. The protocol treats 5% as the boundary of acceptability. The exact null puts it in the upper tail.
The binomial family is fine. Conditioning on the observed scores makes the count Poisson-binomial rather than binomial, since each respondent carries their own \(\alpha_r\). The last two columns show the two standard deviations agree to within a percent throughout. The heterogeneity in \(\alpha_r\) is too small relative to its mean to move the variance, because \(\mathrm{Var}_{\text{PB}} = n\bar\alpha - \sum \alpha_i^2\) differs from \(n\bar\alpha(1-\bar\alpha)\) by \(n\,\mathrm{Var}(\alpha_i)\), which is order \(10^{-4}\) against a mean of order \(10^{-2}\). Marginally, with person locations drawn iid from a latent density, the count is binomial in any case.
So the distributional shape Hagell (2014) investigates is not where the protocol goes wrong. All five of the interval methods compared there are being applied to roughly the right distribution and compared against the wrong number.


Code
dist_one <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA, n = 500) {
  thr <- mk(k, ncat); g <- split_grid(thr, idxA)
  fr <- score_weights(thr, 0, 1.4); fr <- fr / sum(fr)
  p_i <- rep(alpha_by_r(cond_null(g, 0), 1.96), times = round(n * fr))
  d <- pois_binom(p_i)
  data.frame(label = label, prop = 100 * (seq_along(d) - 1L) / length(p_i),
             dens = d)
}
d_cnt <- rbind(
  dist_one("20 items, 4 cat, 10/10", 20, 4, seq(1, 20, by = 2)),
  dist_one("12 items, 4 cat, 6/6",   12, 4, seq(1, 12, by = 2)),
  dist_one("20 items, 2 cat, 10/10", 20, 2, seq(1, 20, by = 2)))

ggplot(subset(d_cnt, prop <= 8), aes(prop, dens, colour = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_step(direction = "mid") +
  labs(x = "Observed significant tests (%)", y = "Exact probability",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

section: 4.9 Extreme-score handling does not rescue it
text:
4.9 Extreme-score handling does not rescue it
The lookup above uses WLE, which is finite at extreme scores. Software using maximum likelihood person estimates has to drop respondents extreme on either subtest, so the check is whether that changes the size.


Code
joint_w <- function(thr_all, idxA, mu = 0, sigma = 1.4, nq = 121L) {
  A <- thr_all[idxA]; B <- thr_all[-idxA]
  q <- seq(mu - 5 * sigma, mu + 5 * sigma, length.out = nq)
  w <- dnorm(q, mu, sigma); w <- w / sum(w)
  Reduce(`+`, Map(function(t, wt) wt * outer(score_dist(A, t), score_dist(B, t)),
                  q, w))
}
chk <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA, mu = 0) {
  thr <- mk(k, ncat); g <- split_grid(thr, idxA)
  W <- joint_w(thr, idxA, mu); W <- W / sum(W)
  sig <- abs(g$t) > 1.96
  keep <- matrix(TRUE, nrow(W), ncol(W))
  keep[c(1L, nrow(W)), ] <- FALSE; keep[, c(1L, ncol(W))] <- FALSE
  data.frame(config = label, all = sum(W * sig),
             pct_ex = 100 * (1 - sum(W[keep])),
             dropped = sum(W[keep] * sig[keep]) / sum(W[keep]))
}
ex <- rbind(
  chk("12 items, 4 cat, 6/6",       12, 4, seq(1, 12, by = 2)),
  chk("20 items, 4 cat, 10/10",     20, 4, seq(1, 20, by = 2)),
  chk("20 items, 4 cat, 4/16",      20, 4, seq(1, 20, by = 5)),
  chk("40 items, 4 cat, 20/20",     40, 4, seq(1, 40, by = 2)),
  chk("20 items, 2 cat, 10/10",     20, 2, seq(1, 20, by = 2)),
  chk("20 items, 4 cat, off target", 20, 4, seq(1, 20, by = 2), mu = -2))
kable(data.frame(ex$config, round(ex$all, 4), round(ex$pct_ex, 1),

title: 4  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
section: 4.10 What this changes about the protocol
text:
4.10 What this changes about the protocol
The protocol’s decision rule compares an observed proportion against 5%. That benchmark is too lenient by a factor of 1.3 to 3.7 across everything tried here, worst on dichotomous items and off-target samples, which are common in health measurement. The direction is uniform, so the protocol is biased toward declaring unidimensionality.
This also gives a mechanism for Hagell’s central finding (Hagell, 2014). Comparing against a benchmark that is too lenient shifts the whole power curve toward passing, so conclusions flipping with sample size is ordinary power behaviour against a biased reference rather than a pathology of the binomial interval. With the correct reference, mild multidimensionality would be rejected at appreciably smaller samples, and larger \(n\) would behave the way it does in any well posed test.
The constructive version is cheap. The enumeration needed to state the correct reference is the same machinery that produced it: one Lord-Wingersky recursion per subtest and one score-to-measure lookup, both of which the package already builds for RMscoreSE(). From that, either report the exact \(\bar\alpha\) and test the observed count against it, or replace 1.96 with the exact per-score critical values so that the 5% benchmark becomes true by construction. The second is closer to what users expect the protocol to mean and needs no change to how results are reported.
crumbs: 4  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol

title: 4  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
section: 4.11 Not yet done: the split is chosen from the data
text:
4.11 Not yet done: the split is chosen from the data
Everything above conditions on a fixed, known split. The protocol chooses the split by principal component analysis of residuals, taking loadings above +0.3 and below -0.3, a cutoff whose rationale Hagell (2014) already calls unclear. That is a selection step, and the null conditional on a data-chosen contrast is not the null for a fixed one. The enumeration therefore understates the size of the protocol as practised.
The two errors run in opposite directions. Referring to 1.96, together with the respondents who cannot be flagged at all, pushes the realised proportion below 5% and makes the protocol too lenient. Selecting the most discrepant contrast pushes it up and makes the protocol too strict. Which dominates depends on item count, response categories, targeting and how unbalanced the split is, and nothing here settles it.
Settling it needs a parametric bootstrap of the whole pipeline: generate under the fitted unidimensional model, run the PCA, take the split, run the t-tests, count. That is the same shape as RMdimResidualPCACutoff() and the infit and Q3 cutoff work, and the exact component above would serve as its reference, which removes most of the noise from the comparison the way the exact RCI null did for the change study.
It is worth holding open that the two errors partly cancel. Existing simulation work reporting the protocol as well behaved under unidimensionality would be consistent with that, and a cancellation would not be stable across the conditions in the first table. I have not checked what Smith (2002) or Horton & Tennant (2010) report on this point, so that reading is a conjecture to verify against the sources rather than a finding of this note.

title: 4  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
text:
4.12 Scope and limits

Complete data only, as in the RCI chapter (Section 7.12). Missing responses break sufficiency of a single subtest score, so the enumeration would run per missingness pattern.
Fixed split. See Section 4.11.
WLE with CML-style thresholds. RUMM2030’s person estimator may differ. It would move the centering column more than the size column, since dropping extremes barely changed the latter.
The latent density enters only through the weighting. The per-score sizes are free of it. Only the sample means and the count distributions depend on the assumed \(N(\mu, \sigma)\).
The 1.96 figure is taken as the rule in force. Software referring to a \(t\) distribution with finite degrees of freedom uses a slightly larger value, which makes the test more conservative, not less.

title: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups
text:
5.1 Purpose
Up to version 1.4.0, RMdifLR() reported Andersen’s likelihood-ratio (LR) test (Andersen, 1973) together with per-group item and threshold locations, and it flagged items whose largest location difference exceeded a fixed cutoff. The locations were centred within each group, so every item was compared with the mean of all items. When the DIF in a test is unbalanced, the mean item moves too, and items without DIF show an apparent difference. This is the artificial DIF described by Andrich & Hagquist (2012).
Comparing items between groups requires an anchor. The scale of a Rasch model has no natural origin, so each group’s item parameters can only be compared after the two scales have been linked. The LR test compares likelihoods and needs no anchor, but every per-item comparison does. After version 1.4.0, RMdifLR() reports only the LR test, and the per-item comparisons moved to the new function RMdifAnchor(). The three studies in this chapter are the evidence behind it. Items are compared through an anchor chosen from the data, each comparison gets a Wald test (Glas & Verhelst, 1995), and the p-values are corrected across items or thresholds.
Study 1 (Section 5.3) covers item locations. Study 2 (Section 5.4) covers thresholds, unequal group sizes, and how much the results depend on random tie-breaks in the anchor selection. Study 3 (Section 5.5) checks a consensus anchor over many tie-breaks. The settings studied differ from the defaults of RMdifAnchor() in a few places, listed in Section 5.6.
crumbs: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups

title: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups
text:
5.2 Background

5.2.1 Anchors
The studies compare three anchors.

Centred. All items, with the locations centred in each group. This is the scale RMdifLR() used up to version 1.4.0. It is equivalent to the equal-mean-difficulty method in Wang (2004). The all-other anchor gives the same z statistics, since an item’s difference from the mean of all items is \((k-1)/k\) times its difference from the mean of the others.
Forward (MTT). The iterative forward class of Kopf et al. (2015a) with the mean test statistic threshold selection of Kopf et al. (2015b). Each item is first tested against several provisional anchors (auxiliary tests), and the items are ranked by how often their test statistic exceeds a threshold based on the mean test statistics. The anchor then grows along this ranking, one item at a time, while it is shorter than the number of items without a significant test against the current anchor (Kopf et al., 2015a). In psychotools the limit is 0.8 times that number, and the top 10% of the ranking are skipped as first candidates. A candidate’s own test is not checked before it enters, so an item with a small shift can enter the anchor.
Gini. The anchor point of Strobl et al. (2021). The second group’s item parameters are shifted along the scale, and the shift that maximises the Gini index of the absolute item-wise differences is chosen. That is the position where a few items differ a lot and the rest overlap. Strobl et al. (2021, Online Appendix F) show that every optimum of the criterion lies where one item’s parameters coincide in the two groups, so the anchor point is always a single anchor item. In psychotools this is anchor(class = "constant", select = "Gini"), which by default has length 1.

Forward and Gini both assume that most items are free of DIF, and this cannot be tested. When a majority of items share the same DIF, treating them as the reference is an equally valid solution (Strobl et al., 2021).
Anchor length is a trade-off. A longer anchor gives more power if it is free of DIF, but a contaminated anchor produces artificial DIF. Teresi & Jones (2016), summarising Wang (2004) and others, report a recommendation of at least four anchor items. The forward anchor grows as long as the data allow. The Gini anchor point is always one item, which Strobl et al. (2021) note may cost power.
Both are computed with psychotools::anchortest() or psychotools::anchor(). The first anchor item fixes the scale and is not tested, so \(k - 1\) items get a test. When items tie in the ranking, psychotools orders them at random. The forward ranking criterion is a count, so ties are common. The Gini criterion is continuous, and ties are rare.


5.2.2 Item locations and thresholds
In the partial credit model, threshold \(k\) of item \(i\) in group \(g\) can be written as
\[
\delta_{ikg} = \beta_{ig} + \tau_{ikg},
\]
where \(\beta_{ig}\) is the item location (the mean of the item’s thresholds) and the \(\tau_{ikg}\) sum to zero within the item. Henninger et al. (2025) distinguish two ways an item can differ between groups. With DIF, every threshold moves by the same amount, so the location moves and the spacing stays the same. With differential step functioning (DSF), the thresholds move by different amounts. Non-symmetric DSF also moves the location. Symmetric DSF leaves the location unchanged and changes only the spacing.
Fixing a group’s scale adds one constant to every \(\delta_{ikg}\) in that group. The constant ends up in \(\beta_{ig}\) and leaves the \(\tau_{ikg}\) unchanged. Group differences in threshold spacing can therefore be tested without an anchor, and they cannot be affected by artificial DIF. Differences in location, and in the thresholds themselves, need an anchor.


5.2.3 Multiplicity correction
Each study tests every item or threshold, so the FWER is the share of datasets where at least one unit without DIF is flagged. The "fwer" correction is the single-step max-|z| adjustment (Hothorn et al., 2008), which uses the correlation between the tests. Holm’s step-down procedure (Holm, 1979) is reported as a check. Kopf et al. (2015a), Kopf et al. (2015b) and Strobl et al. (2021) report per-item false alarm rates for dichotomous items. Wang (2004) showed for partial credit items, as well as dichotomous ones, that the equal-mean-difficulty and all-other methods fail when DIF is unbalanced. Teresi & Jones (2016) note that the Kopf et al. results were for binary Rasch items and that they knew of no such evidence for the graded response model. We did not find a study of the forward or Gini anchors for partial credit items, or of anchor selection followed by a multiplicity correction. These are what the present studies add.

title: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups
text:
5.3 Study 1: item locations

5.3.1 Design
The design has 48 cells with 1000 replications each. Two groups are compared.

Group size. 150, 300 or 600 per group, equal in both groups.
Items. 10 items with 4 categories (locations evenly spaced on [-1.5, 1.5], thresholds at location - 1, location and location + 1), or 20 dichotomous items (locations evenly spaced on [-1.5, 1.5]).
Impact. Group 2’s latent mean is 0 or 0.5. The SD is 1 in both groups.
DIF. None, one item, three items in the same direction, or two items in opposite directions. DIF is uniform: 0.6 logits added to every threshold of the item in group 2. The DIF items are items 3, 6 and 8 of 10, or 5, 11 and 16 of 20. One DIF item is the first of these, and the balanced pair the first two (+0.6 and -0.6).

Each group is fitted by conditional maximum likelihood with psychotools::pcmodel(). Replications with a category unused in either group are skipped, since RMdifLR() and RMdifAnchor() require every category to be used in both groups. Each replication has its own seed. The single-step adjustment is computed with multcomp. The code is in scripts/dif/dif_wald.R (methods) and scripts/dif/dif_wald_sim.R (simulation). The methods match psychotools::anchortest().
With 1000 valid replications, the Monte-Carlo SE of a rate near .05 is about .007, so values from .036 to .064 are consistent with .05. Cells with skipped replications have a wider band, up to .065 with the 840 valid replications of the smallest cell. With many cells, about 2.5% are expected above the band by chance alone.


5.3.2 Calibration without DIF

                 data = nul, FUN = function(x) rng(x))

5.3.3 Family-wise error rate with DIF


Code
ggplot(s1, aes(n, fwer_ss, colour = Anchor, linetype = Anchor, shape = Anchor)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0.036, ymax = 0.064,
           fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_grid(scenario ~ structure + impact_lab, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(scenario = label_wrap_gen(18),
                                 structure = label_wrap_gen(22))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) +
  scale_anchor +
  labs(x = "Respondents per group", y = "Family-wise error rate") +
  theme_dense








Figure 5.1: Study 1, FWER with the single-step correction: the share of datasets where at least one item without DIF is flagged. The grey band is .036 to .064, the range consistent with .05 at 1000 valid replications. Panel rows have separate y-axes.





The centred anchor flags items without DIF as soon as DIF is unbalanced, and more often the larger the sample (Figure 5.1). With three DIF items in the same direction among 10 items (impact 0), the FWER is .239, .470, .870 at 150, 300 and 600 respondents per group. With balanced DIF it holds (.023 to .066).
The forward anchor keeps the FWER at .032 to .070 in every cell but one. The exception is .083, with three DIF items in the same direction among 10 items, 150 respondents per group and impact 0. Strobl et al. (2021) report a per-item false alarm rate “notably above” the nominal 5% for the forward anchor when 40% of 40 dichotomous items had DIF in one direction, in small and medium samples. Their measure and design differ, but the pattern is consistent.
The Gini anchor keeps the FWER well below .05 in most cells (.004 to .027), so some DIF may be missed. It exceeds .05 only in 2 cells, both with three DIF items in the same direction among 10 items and 150 per group (.066 and .071).


5.3.4 Power


Code
pw <- s1[s1$scenario != "No DIF", ]
ggplot(pw, aes(n, power_ss, colour = Anchor, linetype = Anchor, shape = Anchor)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_grid(scenario ~ structure + impact_lab,
             labeller = labeller(scenario = label_wrap_gen(18),
                                 structure = label_wrap_gen(22))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_anchor +
  labs(x = "Respondents per group", y = "Power") +
  theme_dense








Figure 5.2: Study 1, power with the single-step correction: the mean share of DIF items flagged. The untested first anchor item counts as not flagged.





Forward has the highest power when DIF is unbalanced (.874 against .725 for centred, three DIF items among 10, 300 per group). It is close to centred with one DIF item, and below it with balanced DIF (.700 against .840, 150 per group). The centred power comes with the inflated error rate shown above whenever DIF is unbalanced.
Gini has less power than forward in small and medium samples. With one DIF item among 20 dichotomous items and 300 per group, it finds .263 against .562 for forward. With 10 items and 600 per group the two are close (.986 to .995 for Gini). Strobl et al. (2021) also found lower hit rates for the Gini index than for the forward anchor when 20% or 40% of the items had DIF in one direction. With 60% the Gini index had the highest hit rates. In their balanced setting both inequality criteria were outperformed, and they suggest that single-item anchors, which are more affected by sampling error, may play a part.
A DIF item was the untested first anchor item in up to .028 of replications per cell for forward and .084 for Gini.


5.3.5 Run notes
Replications with an unused category in either group were skipped, up to 16% of them (10 items with 4 categories, 150 per group, impact 0.5). Results there are conditional on all categories being used. One of 48,000 replications failed with an error (‘lower’ not specified or contains NA). When a fit fails, RMdifAnchor() stops with a message that names the failing step. The run took 61 minutes on 10 cores.

title: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups
section: 5.4 Study 2: thresholds, unequal group sizes and tie-breaks
text:
5.4 Study 2: thresholds, unequal group sizes and tie-breaks

5.4.1 Design
The design has 144 cells with 1000 replications each.

Group size. A mean of 150, 300 or 600 per group, either equal or unequal (1.5 n and 0.5 n). Group 2 is the smaller, focal group, with the impact and the DIF. Unequal subgroup sizes and differing latent distributions are among the conditions that make DIF detection harder (Teresi & Jones, 2016).
Items. 10 items with 4 categories as in Study 1, or 20 items with 3 categories (thresholds at location ± 0.75). DIF items are at the same positions as in Study 1.
Impact. 0 or 0.5, as in Study 1.
Scenarios, as shifts of group 2’s thresholds per DIF item:

no DIF
uniform DIF in one or three items (every threshold +0.6)
symmetric DSF in one item (lowest threshold -0.6, highest +0.6, location unchanged)
non-symmetric DSF in one or three items (highest threshold +0.6, location +0.2 with three thresholds and +0.3 with two).


Each replication has three families of tests, each with its own correction:

Spacing. A joint Wald test per item of the group differences in adjacent threshold distances, on \(m_i - 1\) df, where \(m_i\) is the number of thresholds of item \(i\). It needs no anchor. Corrections across items: Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg (BH, Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), and a single-step min-p computed from the joint normal of all contrasts.
Anchored thresholds. Each group is shifted so that the mean location of its anchor items is zero, and \(\delta_{ik2} - \delta_{ik1}\) is tested per threshold. Corrections across all thresholds: Holm and single-step max-|z|.
Anchored item locations, as in Study 1. The prototype reproduces psychotools::anchortest() (z identical to within \(10^{-14}\)).

The single-step adjustments are computed by Monte Carlo, with 5000 draws from the joint normal of the estimates. This is the same adjustment as multcomp’s, and it is faster with 30 to 40 correlated tests. On one 10-item dataset, with 20,000 draws, the largest difference from multcomp was .003. With 5000 draws, the Monte-Carlo SE of an adjusted p-value near .05 is about .003.
In the first 250 replications of each cell (fewer valid ones where replications were skipped), the forward and Gini rankings are redone under 20 seeds and compared with the main run. Only the ranking step draws random numbers, so the auxiliary tests are computed once. The Monte-Carlo adjustments use a fixed seed per replication, so a flag can change only through the anchor.
The code is in scripts/dif/dif_thresh.R and scripts/dif/dif_thresh_sim.R.


5.4.2 Results
All results use the single-step correction unless stated. Figures show impact 0. Across matched cells, impact 0.5 changed the FWER by at most .027 for the forward and Gini anchors and the spacing test.

5.4.2.1 Spacing tests


Code
sp <- sm[sm$family == "spacing" & sm$correction != "none" & sm$impact == 0, ]
sp$Correction <- factor(sp$correction, levels = c("ss", "holm", "bh"),
                        labels = c("Single-step", "Holm", "BH"))
sp_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(sp[c("n", "Scenario", "Items", "Sizes", "Correction")],
             what = "FWER", value = sp$fwer),
  data.frame(sp[c("n", "Scenario", "Items", "Sizes", "Correction")],
             what = "Power", value = sp$power))
sp_long <- sp_long[!is.na(sp_long$value), ]
sp_long <- sp_long[sp_long$what == "FWER" | sp_long$Scenario == "Symmetric DSF, 1 item", ]
sp_long <- aggregate(value ~ n + Items + Sizes + Correction + what, data = sp_long, FUN = mean)
sp_long$panel <- interaction(sp_long$Items, sp_long$Sizes, sep = "\n")
cor_cols <- c("Single-step" = "#0072B2", "Holm" = "#CC79A7", "BH" = "#D55E00")
cor_lty <- c("Single-step" = "solid", "Holm" = "dashed", "BH" = "dotted")
cor_shp <- c("Single-step" = 16, "Holm" = 17, "BH" = 4)
band <- data.frame(what = "FWER", ymin = 0.036, ymax = 0.064, y = 0.05)
ggplot(sp_long, aes(n, value, colour = Correction, linetype = Correction,
                    shape = Correction)) +
  geom_rect(data = band, aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(data = band, aes(yintercept = y), colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(what ~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cor_cols) + scale_linetype_manual(values = cor_lty) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = cor_shp) +
  labs(x = "Respondents per group (mean)", y = NULL) +
  theme_dense








Figure 5.3: Study 2, spacing tests (no anchor), impact 0. Top: FWER, the share of datasets where at least one item without a spacing difference is flagged, averaged over the six scenarios (items with uniform DIF have unchanged spacing and count as null). The grey band is .036 to .064. Bottom: power to detect the one symmetric DSF item.





The spacing test needs no anchor, and its error rate does not depend on the DIF scenario (Figure 5.3). The FWER is .011 to .059 with the single-step correction and .009 to .055 with Holm, over all 144 cells. BH controls the false discovery rate, not the FWER. Without DSF it behaves like the others, but with a DSF item in the test its FWER goes up to .092.
Power depends on how the thresholds move. One symmetric DSF item is found in .762 to .923 of datasets with 600 per group, and in .530 to .822 with unequal groups of 900 and 300. A non-symmetric shift of one threshold is harder to see in the spacing (.148 to .413 at 600), where only the highest threshold moves and so only the last distance changes.


5.4.2.2 Anchored tests: error rate


Code
fw <- ss[ss$family != "spacing" & ss$impact == 0, ]
fw$Family <- factor(fw$family, levels = c("locations", "thresholds"),
                    labels = c("Locations", "Thresholds"))
fw$panel <- paste0(sub("x", " x ", fw$structure), "\n", fw$ratio, " n")
ggplot(fw, aes(n, fwer, colour = Anchor, linetype = Anchor, shape = Anchor)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0.036, ymax = 0.064,
           fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_grid(Scenario ~ Family + panel, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(Scenario = label_wrap_gen(14))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) +
  scale_anchor +
  labs(x = "Respondents per group (mean)", y = "Family-wise error rate") +
  theme_dense +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7), axis.text = element_text(size = 6),
        panel.spacing = unit(0.25, "cm"))








Figure 5.4: Study 2, anchored tests, impact 0: FWER with the single-step correction for item locations (left four columns) and thresholds (right four). Columns: 10 x 4 = 10 items with 4 categories, 20 x 3 = 20 items with 3 categories, equal or unequal group sizes. The grey band is .036 to .064 (1000 valid replications). Panel rows have separate y-axes.





The centred scale fails as in Study 1 (Figure 5.4). With three uniform DIF items among 10 (equal groups, impact 0), its FWER for item locations is .199, .482, .863 at 150, 300 and 600 per group, and for thresholds .079, .147, .285.
Without DIF, the forward anchor has an FWER of .029 to .074 for locations and .015 to .059 for thresholds. Over all scenarios, 17 of 144 location cells and 4 of 144 threshold cells are above the band for their number of valid replications, against about 3.6 per family expected by chance. The location cells above the band are 3 without DIF, 6 with three uniform DIF items, 2 with one symmetric DSF item, 6 with three non-symmetric DSF items. The largest values are in two kinds of cells.

Non-symmetric DSF in three items. Each such item moves its location by only 0.2 or 0.3 logits, which the forward selection often misses. At 600 per group, a DSF item is in the anchor in .333 to .896 of datasets, and the location FWER is .049 to .097.
Three uniform DIF items with small samples. With 10 items and 150 per group, a DIF item is in the anchor in .422 to .582 of datasets, and the location FWER is .071 to .077.

In both, DIF items enter the anchor. With uniform DIF of 0.6 the selection removes them as n grows (a DIF item is in the anchor in .003 to .014 of datasets at 600 per group), and the inflation goes away. The small location shifts of non-symmetric DSF stay in the anchor more often. With 10 items the inflation then grows with n, because the tests get more precise (.043, .069, .097 at 150, 300 and 600 per group, equal groups). With 20 items it does not (.056, .072, .055).
The Gini anchor flags units without DIF less often than the nominal 5%. Without DIF its FWER is .005 to .020 for locations and .012 to .035 for thresholds, and over all scenarios it is above the band in 3 of 144 location cells and 0 of 144 threshold cells (maximum .070).
Without DIF, unequal group sizes did not change the calibration. The forward location FWER averaged .052 with equal and .049 with unequal groups.


5.4.2.3 Anchored tests: power


Code
pw2 <- ss[ss$family != "spacing" & ss$impact == 0 & ss$ratio == "equal" &
            ss$scenario != "null" & !is.na(ss$power), ]
pw2$Family <- factor(pw2$family, levels = c("locations", "thresholds"),
                     labels = c("Locations", "Thresholds"))
ggplot(pw2, aes(n, power, colour = Anchor, linetype = Anchor, shape = Anchor)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(Scenario ~ Family + Items,
             labeller = labeller(Scenario = label_wrap_gen(14))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_anchor +
  labs(x = "Respondents per group", y = "Power") +
  theme_dense








Figure 5.5: Study 2, anchored tests, equal group sizes, impact 0: power with the single-step correction, the mean share of DIF units flagged. For locations a unit is an item with a location shift, for thresholds a shifted threshold. Symmetric DSF does not move the location, so it has no location power. For locations, the untested first anchor item counts as not flagged. Every threshold is tested.





For item locations the pattern is that of Study 1 (Figure 5.5). Forward is as powerful as centred with one DIF item and more powerful with three (.883 against .731, 10 items, 300 per group), and Gini has less power than forward (.758 in the same cell, and .831 against .968 with one DIF item).
Threshold tests need more data. One threshold shifted by 0.6 is found in .773 of datasets with 10 items and 600 per group under the forward anchor, and in .130 with 150. The threshold test spreads its error rate over 30 or 40 thresholds, so for uniform DIF it is much weaker than the location test (.232 against .968, one DIF item, 300 per group).
Unequal sizes cost power. With the same total n, the threshold power of the forward anchor at 600 per group (900 and 300) was 61% to 81% of that with equal groups.


5.4.2.4 Dependence on the tie-break


Code
tt <- aggregate(cbind(unique_sets, set_diff, loc_any_change, thr_any_change) ~ anchor,
                data = tie, FUN = function(x) rng(x))
tt$anchor <- c(forward = "Forward (MTT)", gini = "Gini")[tt$anchor]
tt$unique_sets <- aggregate(unique_sets ~ anchor, data = tie,
  FUN = function(x) paste0(formatC(min(x), format = "f", digits = 1), " to ",
                           formatC(max(x), format = "f", digits = 1)))$unique_sets
names(tt) <- c("Anchor", "Distinct anchor sets", "Seeds giving another set",
               "Location flags change", "Threshold flags change")
kable(tt)

Distinct anchor sets: mean number of different anchor sets over the 20 seeds. Seeds giving another set: mean share of seeds whose anchor set differs from that of the main run. Flags change: share of datasets where some seed changes which units are flagged (single-step).

The forward anchor depends on the random tie-break in every condition (Table 5.2). Over 20 seeds it gives 3.6 to 9.3 different anchor sets per dataset on average, and in .563 to .790 of seeds the untested first anchor item differs from the main run’s. Without DIF these differences rarely change a flag (location flags change in .004 to .053 of datasets). With DIF they do. With three uniform DIF items, some seed changes a threshold flag in .071 to .612 of datasets, and the largest value, .612, is at 600 per group (10 items with 4 categories, equal sizes, impact 0.5). The number of true DIF units found also varies by seed, in up to 41% of datasets for locations and 60% for thresholds.
Ties are rare for the Gini anchor point. In .000 to .012 of seeds the anchor item differed, and flags changed in at most 1% of datasets.


5.4.2.5 Run notes
Replications with an unused category in either group were skipped, up to 47% of them (10x4, mean 150 per group, unequal sizes, impact 0.5). These are the cells where the smaller group has 75 respondents, and their results are conditional on all categories being used. Six of 144,000 replications failed with an error (infinite or missing values in ‘x’). The run took 42 minutes on 10 cores.

title: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups
text:
5.5 Study 3: a consensus forward anchor

5.5.1 Design
Study 2 showed that the forward anchor depends on the random order of tied items. Study 3 checks whether a consensus over many seeds removes that dependence. For each dataset, the ranking is redone under S seeds, and each item’s inclusion frequency is the share of seeds whose anchor contains it. The consensus anchor is the items with an inclusion frequency of at least .5. The auxiliary tests are computed once per dataset, so extra seeds are cheap.
Two rules are compared for the untested reference item. In the first, it is the anchor item that is most often first in the per-seed anchors, as psychotools leaves the first anchor item untested. In the second (“all items tested”), every item is tested when the anchor has two or more items. An anchor item’s difference from the anchor mean is a well-defined contrast, and the single-step adjustment handles the singular covariance. But the anchor items were chosen because they looked free of DIF in the same data, so their tests lean towards non-rejection, and they add tests to the max-|z| family. The results show the net effect.
To measure reproducibility, each dataset is analysed with two disjoint sets of 200 seeds, and the results are compared for S = 1 (the single-seed forward anchor), 50, 100 and 200 seeds within each set.
The design is that of Study 2 with impact 0 only (72 cells, 1000 replications each), since impact changed the Study 2 error rates by at most .027. The datasets are the impact-0 datasets of Study 2. As a check, the Gini results of all 144 cell and family combinations agree with Study 2 to within .001 in FWER and .002 in power. The code is in scripts/dif/dif_consensus.R and scripts/dif/dif_consensus_sim.R, which also source scripts/dif/dif_thresh.R.


5.5.2 Results


Code
cal <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(m3, m3$Method), function(d) {
  lo <- d[d$family == "locations", ]
  th <- d[d$family == "thresholds", ]

             loc_fwer = mx(lo$fwer), thr_fwer = mx(th$fwer),
             loc_pow = r3(mean(lo$power, na.rm = TRUE)),
             thr_pow = r3(mean(th$power, na.rm = TRUE)),
             len = formatC(mean(lo$anchor_len), format = "f", digits = 1))
}))
names(cal) <- c("Anchor", "FWER, locations", "FWER, thresholds",
                "Power, locations", "Power, thresholds", "Anchor items")
kable(cal, row.names = FALSE)

  labs(x = "Respondents per group (mean)", y = "Threshold flags differ",
       colour = NULL, linetype = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_dense +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))








Figure 5.6: Study 3: share of datasets where two seed sets flag different thresholds, for the single-seed forward anchor and the consensus over 200 seeds. Mean over item structures and group-size ratios.





The consensus reduces the dependence on the seed but does not remove it (Table 5.4, Figure 5.6). Two single seeds flag different thresholds in .037 of datasets on average, and in up to .267 per cell. Two sets of 200 seeds disagree in .011 on average, and in up to .056. Most of the gain comes with the first 50 seeds.
The remaining disagreement does not come from too few seeds. It comes from items whose inclusion frequency is close to .5, so that the forward anchor contains them under about half of the possible orderings. With 200 seeds, .072 of all items had an inclusion frequency between .4 and .6, and 44% of datasets had at least one such item. In those datasets the two seed sets gave different flags in .041 of cases, and in the others in .002. More seeds estimate the frequency of such an item more precisely, but it stays near the cut.
The most-often-first rule does not give a stable reference item. The two seed sets chose the same one in .475 of datasets, because the first position is spread over several tied items. Testing all items avoids the choice.
Replications with an unused category were skipped as in Study 2 (up to 24% per cell). One of 72,000 replications failed with an error. The run took 134 minutes on 10 cores.

title: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups
section: 5.6 Simulated settings and the defaults of RMdifAnchor()
text:
5.6 Simulated settings and the defaults of RMdifAnchor()
The studies were run before RMdifAnchor() was written, and its defaults differ from the simulated settings in three places.

Forward anchor. Studies 1 and 2 used one tie-break ordering per dataset. RMdifAnchor() uses the consensus of Study 3, the items in the anchor under at least half of n_seeds = 100 orderings.
Untested item. Studies 1 and 2, and the consensus rows of Study 3 except “all tested”, leave the first anchor item untested, as psychotools::anchortest() does. RMdifAnchor() tests every item when the anchor has two or more items. With the Gini anchor point, the single anchor item is untested in both.
Single-step adjustment. Study 1 used multcomp, and Studies 2 and 3 used 5000 Monte-Carlo draws. RMdifAnchor() uses 10,000 draws, so the Monte-Carlo SE of an adjusted p-value near .05 is about .002 instead of .003.

The default combination, 100 seeds with every item tested, was not simulated. Study 3 covers each part separately: 100 seeds with the reference item untested, and 200 seeds with every item tested. Their results are close. The location FWER had a mean of .051 and a maximum of .085 with 100 seeds, against .048 and .083 with 200 seeds and every item tested. Two disjoint seed sets flagged different thresholds in .012 and .011 of datasets, and in .011 with 200 seeds and the reference item untested. Above 100 seeds the number of seeds matters little, so the defaults are expected to behave like the “all tested” row.

title: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups
text:
5.7 Interpretation

The centred scale should not be used to test or flag single items or thresholds. Its error rate depends on whether DIF is balanced, which cannot be known from the data.
The spacing test needs no anchor and kept the FWER at or below the Monte-Carlo band around .05 in every scenario, with the single-step correction or Holm. It answers a narrower question, whether the distances between thresholds differ, and it needs large groups to detect one DSF item.
The forward (MTT) anchor with the single-step correction kept the FWER close to .05 in most cells and had the highest power among the anchors that held the FWER. Its FWER exceeded the band, up to .097, when several items carried small location shifts that the selection missed, and with three uniform DIF items in small samples. Its results depend on the random tie-break: with the same data, another seed often gives another anchor, and with DIF present it changes which units are flagged in a noticeable share of datasets. A consensus over 50 or more seeds keeps the error rates and power. Two independent seed sets then flag different thresholds in .011 of datasets on average, against .037 for two single seeds (Study 3). The rest comes from items that the forward anchor includes under about half of the orderings, and more seeds do not remove it. Reporting each item’s inclusion frequency shows when this is the case. Testing all items avoids an unstable reference item.
The Gini anchor point flags units without DIF less often than the nominal 5% (FWER up to .035 without DIF), so some DIF is missed. It has less power than forward in small and medium samples, and is effectively deterministic. Its value remains the criterion plot (Strobl et al., 2021).
Threshold-level tests have much lower power than location tests for uniform DIF, because the error rate is spread over all thresholds. Location tests and the spacing test together cover uniform DIF and symmetric DSF. Anchored threshold tests add information mainly for non-symmetric DSF.

title: 5  Anchored DIF tests for two groups
text:
5.8 Not covered
More than two groups, DIF sizes other than 0.6, non-uniform DIF in the sense of unequal discrimination (outside the partial credit model), unequal group sizes for dichotomous items, anchors of a length fixed in advance, and anchor rules that would resolve items with an inclusion frequency near .5.

title: 6  The practical impact of DIF
text:
6.1 Purpose
RMdifAnchor() and RMdifTree() answer whether items function differently between groups. With a few hundred respondents per group, a DIF test can flag items whose DIF has no practical consequence, and with small groups it can miss DIF that matters. Statistical significance and practical importance are separate questions (Meade, 2010). RMdifImpact() answers the second: once DIF has been flagged, is it large enough that something should be done about it?
The consequence of DIF depends on what the scale is used for. Two uses are studied here.
Three ways of handling a DIF item are compared. Keep ignores the DIF and scores everyone with pooled item parameters. Remove drops the item. Split gives the item group-specific parameters, anchored through the other items.
Study 1 computes the population values of the bias for each strategy, without simulation, over a broad grid of scales. Study 2 simulates the estimates from one dataset, both when the true DIF items are known and when they are the items RMdifAnchor() flags. Study 3 covers the other outputs of RMdifImpact(): the impact of each DIF item separately, classification rates at a cut-off, and projection to another population.

title: 6  The practical impact of DIF
text:
Group comparison. How much does the DIF bias the estimated difference between the groups’ means?
Individual scores. How much does it shift persons in one group relative to persons with the same latent value in the other group, where on the scale is the shift largest, and how does it change who is classified above a cut-off?
crumbs: 6  The practical impact of DIF

title: 6  The practical impact of DIF
text:
6.2 Background

6.2.1 Model and estimand
Items follow the partial credit model. DIF is uniform: every threshold of a DIF item is shifted by the same number of logits in the focal group, so the item is harder for focal persons with the same \(\theta\). This shift is the DIF size, written as, for example, DIF = 0.5 logits. The latent distributions are \(N(0, 1)\) in the reference group and \(N(\mu_f, 1)\) in the focal group.
The target is the group difference \(\Delta = \mu_f - \mu_r\). Three estimators of \(\Delta\) are compared.

WLE mean. The difference between the groups’ mean weighted likelihood estimates (Warm, 1989).
Latent mean. Item parameters fixed at their CML estimates, and each group’s mean and SD estimated by marginal maximum likelihood. For Rasch-family items the marginal likelihood depends on a response pattern only through its raw score.
Sum score. The difference in mean raw scores. Under split, the focal group’s raw scores are first equated to the reference items through the test characteristic curves, \(T_r^{-1}(T_f(\cdot))\).

Every estimator has some bias without DIF (the WLE through extreme scores, the sum score through floor and ceiling), and that bias differs between \(k\) and \(k - 1\) items. The impact of a strategy is therefore defined as its estimate of \(\Delta\) under DIF minus the same strategy’s estimate for the same persons without DIF. Remove and split have zero impact when the anchor items are free of DIF. Keep does not.


6.2.2 Group-level bias under keep
When a DIF item is kept, its pooled parameters lie between the two groups’ true values. To first order, the bias in \(\Delta\) is \(-\text{DIF}\) times the item’s share of the test information, averaged over the persons,
\[
\text{bias}(\hat\Delta_\text{keep}) \approx -\text{DIF} \, \overline{I_j(\theta) / I(\theta)},
\]
where \(I_j\) is the item’s information and \(I\) the test information. The bias does not shrink as \(n\) grows. The standard error of \(\hat\Delta\) does, so the same DIF distorts the comparison more in a larger study. A bias that is negligible as an effect size can still make a confidence interval for \(\Delta\) miss its target in a large study, and the two readings must be kept apart.


6.2.3 Local bias
The information share of an item varies with \(\theta\), so the shift is local. A focal person at \(\theta\) has the expected raw score \(T_f(\theta)\), which a reference person reaches at \(T_r^{-1}(T_f(\theta))\). The local bias
\[
b(\theta) = T_r^{-1}\big(T_f(\theta)\big) - \theta
\]
is the horizontal distance between the groups’ test characteristic curves, in logits. It is the difference in estimated \(\theta\) between a focal and a reference person with the same true \(\theta\). Divided by the standard error of measurement (SEM) at \(\theta\), it is the shift in SEM units. The vertical distance \(T_f(\theta) - T_r(\theta)\) is the expected raw-score difference at equal \(\theta\), which Chalmers et al. (2016) integrate over \(\theta\) as signed and unsigned measures of differential test functioning.
An item targeted at a high cut-off can have a small group-mean bias and a large local bias at the cut, since the item carries a large share of the information there and little elsewhere. An off-target item is the only informative item in its region, so its share keeps rising into the tail. The local summaries are therefore restricted to the central 95% of the pooled latent distribution. They are the local bias where its absolute value is largest, its location, and \(b\) at a cut-off.


6.2.4 Estimating the impact from one dataset
Given the items to split, the impact is estimated within one dataset as \(\hat\Delta_\text{keep} - \hat\Delta_\text{split}\) for each estimator. The split model is fitted by conditional maximum likelihood with one shift parameter per split item, and the local bias is computed from its parameters over the estimated latent mixture. Standard errors come from the delta method on the estimated DIF sizes \(\widehat{\text{DIF}}\), with the other item parameters treated as fixed. The difference \(\hat\Delta_\text{keep} -
\hat\Delta_\text{remove}\) is not used, since it also carries the difference in estimator bias between \(k\) and \(k - 1\) items.
Treating the other item parameters as fixed is an approximation. In the population calculation of Study 1, the variance from the shifts alone was a median of 94% of the full parameter variance of \(\hat\Delta_\text{split}\). Studies 2 and 3 check the resulting intervals directly.

title: 6  The practical impact of DIF
text:
6.3 Study 1: population values

6.3.1 Design
No data are simulated. Each model is fitted by CML to the expected sufficient statistics (category counts and raw-score distribution in each group, from quadrature over the true latent distributions). This gives the probability limit of every estimate. The SE at given group sizes combines the sampling error of the estimator and the delta-method error from the item parameters. The grid has 216 settings.

Items. 5, 10 or 20 dichotomous items (locations evenly spaced on \([-2, 2]\)), or 5, 10 or 20 items with four categories (locations evenly spaced on \([-1.5, 1.5]\), thresholds at location \(-1\), \(0\) and \(+1\)).
DIF item. One item, either the most central or the one with the largest location (off target).
DIF size. 0.5, 0.8 or 1.2 logits.
Focal mean. \(\mu_f\) = 0 or 0.5.
Group sizes. 500/500, 1000/200 or 2000/100 (reference/focal).



6.3.2 Results
Size of the bias under keep. Figure 6.1 shows the population impact of keeping the item on the latent mean difference. For a central four-category item with DIF = 0.5 it is 0.121 logits at 5 items, 0.059 at 10 and 0.029 at 20, roughly halving each time the scale doubles in length. An off-target item has a smaller group-mean bias, because few persons are in the region where it carries information. The first-order formula is close for central items (ratio first-order/exact 0.92 to 1.14), but it overstates the bias of off-target items (up to 1.44), so RMdifImpact() computes the impact from the fitted models instead.








Figure 6.1: Study 1. Population bias in the latent mean difference when the DIF item is kept, by DIF size, number of items, item type and position. Focal mean 0.5, groups 500/500 (the bias hardly depends on group size). The dotted line is zero.





Size on the reference scales. A bias in logits does not say whether it matters. Figure 6.2 expresses the same bias on the four scales that RMdifImpact() reports.

Share of the group difference, \(|\text{impact}| / \Delta\). Here \(\Delta\) = 0.5. The scale depends on the true difference: the same bias is two and a half times as large a share of a difference of 0.2. In one dataset RMdifImpact() divides by \(\hat\Delta_\text{split}\), which has no DIF bias.
Standardised mean difference (SMD), the impact divided by the square root of the average of the two group variances. With unit latent SDs it is close to the bias in logits.
Largest local bias in SEM units, the largest value of \(|b(\theta)| / \text{SEM}(\theta)\) over the central 95% of the latent distribution. This is the scale for individual scores.
Bias in SE units, the bias divided by the SE of \(\hat\Delta\). It depends on the group sizes and sets the coverage in Figure 6.3. It is shown at 500/500.

For a central four-category item in a five-item scale, DIF = 0.5 removes 24% of the group difference (SMD 0.12), and DIF = 1.2 removes 57% (SMD 0.27), a bias of 4.0 SEs at 500/500. The same DIF moves a focal person’s estimate by at most 0.23 and 0.53 SEM. The group comparison is affected far more than the individual scores. A longer scale dilutes both, but not equally. From 5 to 20 items at DIF = 1.2, the share of \(\Delta\) falls from 57% to 14%, and the largest local bias in SEM units only from 0.53 to 0.26, because the SEM also shrinks as items are added.
An off-target item has the smaller group-level bias (39% of \(\Delta\) at five items and DIF = 1.2) but the larger local bias in SEM units (0.63), at the edge of the range. Dichotomous items give similar shares of \(\Delta\) (62% for a central item at five items and DIF = 1.2) and smaller values in SEM units (0.32), since the SEM of a dichotomous scale is larger.
None of the scales has a value below which a bias is negligible in general. Which one matters depends on the use: the share of \(\Delta\) and the SMD for a group comparison, the bias in SE units for whether a confidence interval for \(\Delta\) can be trusted in a study of a given size, and the SEM scale for individual scores.








Figure 6.2: Study 1. Bias under keep on four reference scales, four-category items, focal mean 0.5 (Δ = 0.5), latent mean estimator. Rows: share of the group difference (%), standardised mean difference, largest local bias over the central 95% of the latent distribution in SEM units, and bias in SE units of the estimated difference at 500/500. All in absolute value. Each row has its own y axis. Values for central items in Table 6.5.





Consequence for a group comparison. Figure 6.3 shows the coverage of a nominal 95% confidence interval for \(\Delta\) when the item is kept, computed from the bias and the total SE at each sample size. With five items and DIF = 0.5, coverage is .63 at 500/500, .74 at 1000/200 and .83 at 2000/100. The equal-groups design has the smallest SE for \(\Delta\) and is hit hardest. At 20 items and DIF = 0.5 the coverage is .93 to .94. The bias in SE units, which sets the coverage, is about the same for the three estimators (ratio latent/WLE 0.94 to 1.04, sum score/WLE 0.86 to 1.09), so the choice of estimator does not change the conclusion.








Figure 6.3: Study 1. Coverage of a nominal 95% confidence interval for the latent mean difference when the DIF item is kept. Central item, focal mean 0.5. Columns are reference/focal group sizes. The dotted line is .95.





Split against remove. Both have zero impact. The question is precision. The split item cannot inform \(\Delta\), which is identified through the common items, and the error in \(\widehat{\text{DIF}}\) is shared by every focal person, so it does not average out. For the latent mean the SE of \(\hat\Delta\) is the same under split and remove (largest ratio 1.004). For the WLE mean and the sum score, in SMD units, split has a larger SE at five items (largest ratio for the WLE: 1.13 dichotomous, 1.05 four categories) and practically the same at 20 items (1.007). Split is never more than 0.5% more precise than remove, so for a group comparison removing the item costs no more than splitting it. Both lose the item’s information about the group difference. Compared with keeping the item, this widens the SE of the latent mean difference by 2 to 10% at five items and by at most 2% at 20 items, much less than the loss in reliability, since that SE is dominated by the variance between persons.
Local against group-mean bias. The largest absolute local bias over the central 95% of the latent distribution is 1.0 to 1.4 times the group-mean bias for central items and 2.0 to 3.6 times for off-target items. For off-target items the largest local bias is at the edge of the range, so its value depends on how the range is defined, and it has to be reported with its location.

text:
6.4 Study 2: estimates from one dataset

6.4.1 Design
The simulation checks the estimates RMdifImpact() reports: their bias, their delta-method SE, and the coverage of their confidence intervals. It also covers what happens when the items to split are those RMdifAnchor() flags instead of the true DIF items. Study 1 covers the range of scale types, so the simulation is restricted to four-category items (thresholds as in Study 1), a focal mean of 0.5 and a cut-off at \(\theta\) = 1. The scenarios are in Table 6.1. Each is crossed with DIF = 0.5 or 0.8 and group sizes 250/250, 500/500 or 800/200, giving 42 cells with 1000 replications each.

Each replication draws a dataset with DIF and a twin without DIF from the same persons and the same uniform random numbers, so only the DIF items’ focal-group responses differ. The twin gives the counterfactual for the true impact of each strategy and a no-DIF dataset for false flags. In each replication:

Strategies. Keep, remove and split (with the true DIF items) are fitted and linked to the true metric through the DIF-free items. The group difference is estimated with each of the three estimators, and WLEs are scored for every person.
Estimates. The impact \(\hat\Delta_\text{keep} - \hat\Delta_\text{split}\) and the local-bias summaries are computed with their delta-method SEs, for the true DIF items and for the items RMdifAnchor() flags with its defaults (forward consensus anchor, item level, single-step correction at .05). Both are computed on the DIF dataset and on its twin.

The targets are the population values for each cell, computed as in Study 1. No replication failed.


6.4.2 Population pattern
Figure 6.4 shows the local bias for each scenario. For a central item, \(b(\theta)\) is close to its minimum over most of the range, and the group-mean bias describes it well. For an item near the cut, the bias grows toward the item and beyond it, and the largest value is at the upper edge of the range. With two opposite items the group-mean bias nearly cancels, while each item creates a local bias in its own region of the scale.








Figure 6.4: Population local bias b(θ): the difference in estimated θ between a focal and a reference person with the same true θ, when the DIF items are kept. Short horizontal segments on the right edge mark the group-mean bias (latent mean) for each DIF size. The shaded band is the central 95% of the latent distribution at 500/500, the vertical dotted line the cut at θ = 1.







6.4.3 Estimates with the true DIF items
With the true DIF items split, the estimates are close to unbiased, and the delta-method confidence intervals are near nominal (Figure 6.5). The SE ratio is the mean delta-method SE divided by the empirical SD over replications. A coverage of .95 has a Monte Carlo SE of .007 at 1000 replications. The lowest coverages for the impact (.90 to .92) are at DIF = 0.8 with items near the cut, where the delta method on \(\widehat{\text{DIF}}\) alone understates the SD by up to 15%. A bootstrap is not needed for these estimates.








Figure 6.5: Study 2. Coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals (left) and SE ratio, the mean delta-method SE divided by the empirical SD (right), with the true DIF items split, DIF data. One point per cell, jittered vertically. Two opposite: the scenario with two DIF items in opposite directions. Grey band: .95 ± two Monte Carlo SEs. The smallest local bias is shown for DIF in one direction only. Values, with the largest absolute bias, in Table 6.6.





Two quantities need care.

Maxima of curves that cross zero. The largest absolute value of a noisy curve is biased upward when the true curve crosses zero, as it does with two opposite items. The bias is small (at most 0.011 logits against targets of 0.086 to 0.154), and the SE is too large as well, so the coverage stays above .95.
The least affected end of the range. For DIF in one direction, the smallest local bias is found at the edge of the range farthest from the item. Its intervals cover .72 to .92. The delta method holds the range fixed, but the range comes from the estimated latent distribution, and at that edge \(b(\theta)\) changes fast relative to its small value. The largest local bias is not affected in the same way, even when it is at the other edge. RMdifImpact() therefore reports the local bias where its absolute value is largest, with its location, and the value at the cut, but not the smallest.

Split against remove. The simulation confirms Study 1 (Table 6.2). In raw points, the sum score’s SE ratio is misleading, since remove has one item less. Relative to the size of the difference (\(SE/|\Delta|\), which sets the power), split and remove are equally precise for all three estimators.

The bias is small compared with the measurement error. Keep and split have about the same RMSE against the true \(\theta\) (ratio split/keep 0.96 to 1.06), and remove has a 4 to 17% larger RMSE. 6.4.4 Detection by RMdifAnchor()
Figure 6.6 shows how often RMdifAnchor() flags every true DIF item (other items may be flagged as well). At DIF = 0.5 with 250/250 or 800/200, a single item is flagged in 55 to 86% of datasets. When there are two DIF items near the cut, both are flagged in only 14 to 52% of datasets at those sizes. At least one item without DIF is flagged in 5 to 11% of the DIF datasets with five items, where four anchor items carry artificial DIF (Andrich & Hagquist, 2012), and in 3 to 6% with ten items. On the no-DIF twins, some item is flagged in 3.2 to 6.6% of datasets, against a nominal family-wise rate of 5%. RMdifAnchor() stops when a response category is unused in one group, which happened in up to 16% of the DIF datasets, most often with a focal group of 200.








Figure 6.6: Study 2. Share of datasets where RMdifAnchor() flags all true DIF items (other items may also be flagged). The x axis is reference/focal group sizes.







6.4.5 Estimates with the flagged items
What goes wrong with the flagged items is the item set, not the estimate (Figure 6.7). Datasets where nothing was flagged are left out, since the function would not be used there.








Figure 6.7: Study 2. Estimates computed for the items RMdifAnchor() flagged, DIF data, by what was flagged. Exact: all DIF items and nothing else. Item missed: a DIF item not flagged, and no false flag. False flag: at least one item without DIF flagged. Left: share of all datasets in a cell. Middle and right: coverage of the population target by the 95% confidence interval, for the latent-mean impact and the largest absolute local bias. One point per cell with at least 10 datasets in the class, jittered vertically. The diamond is the median. Values in Table 6.7.






Exact set. The estimates behave as with the true items. In the cells with the lowest power the impact is slightly too large in absolute value (relative bias up to 15% with one item), the usual inflation after selection on significance.
A DIF item missed. The estimate covers only the items it is given. With two items in the same direction it is about half the true impact (mean −0.074 to −0.050 against −0.168 to −0.105). With two opposite items it is one item’s impact without the other’s cancelling contribution (−0.083 to −0.021 against −0.026 to −0.010). The largest local bias is then less wrong, because the two items act in different regions of the scale.
A false flag. With five items, the falsely flagged item carries apparent DIF in the opposite direction to the real one. Splitting it as well pulls the estimate toward zero, and in the worst cell past it (the mean estimate is off by 119% of the impact).



6.4.6 False flags without DIF
When RMdifAnchor() flags an item in a no-DIF twin, the impact estimate for that item is not zero, and its confidence interval excludes zero in most of these datasets (Table 6.4). The item was flagged because its estimated shift was large, and the estimated impact is roughly the shift times the item’s information share. The impact interval therefore restates the DIF test and adds no evidence that the DIF exists. What it adds is the size. With ten items, a false flag gives an impact about half that of a real item with DIF = 0.5. With five items, the upper tail reaches the size of a real one.

title: 6  The practical impact of DIF
section: 6.5 Study 3: per-item impacts, rates at a cut and projection
text:
6.5 Study 3: per-item impacts, rates at a cut and projection

6.5.1 Design
Study 3 covers the other outputs of RMdifImpact(), with the true DIF items and the DIF data of the same 42 cells as Study 2.

Per-item impact. With two DIF items, the impact of keeping item \(j\) while the other DIF item stays split, \(\Delta_{\text{split } S \setminus j} - \Delta_{\text{split } S}\), where \(S\) is the set of DIF items. It shows how much of the total impact each item carries.
Rates at a cut. Persons are classified as at or above a cut at \(\theta\) = 1, either by their WLE or by their sum score. The sum-score cut is the raw score nearest the reference group’s expected score at \(\theta\) = 1, and on that scale a person’s true status is a \(\theta\) at or above the point where the reference group’s expected score is the cut minus 0.5. Under split, the focal group’s WLEs come from its own item parameters, and its raw scores are equated to the reference group by true-score equating. A focal person then counts as at or above a sum-score cut when the equated score is at or above the cut minus 0.5, that is, when the nearest whole score is at or above the cut. Comparing the equated score with the cut itself would move the focal cut by a whole raw score for any DIF, however small, that makes the items easier for the focal group. For each group and strategy, three rates are given as shares of the group: classified at or above the cut, false negatives (true status at or above the cut, classified below) and false positives (true status below the cut, classified at or above). The difference keep − split is given as well. The rates are computed from the split model and each group’s estimated normal latent distribution, not counted among the persons in the sample.
Projection. The impact, the SE of \(\hat\Delta\) in a study of the target’s size, the bias in those SE units, and the rates, for a target population of 40 000 reference persons from \(N(0, 1)\) and 10 000 focal persons from \(N(0.25, 1.25^2)\). It differs from every simulated cell.

The outputs were simulated in three parts. The projected impact and its size in SE units come from 1000 replications per cell. The rates at the \(\theta\) cut and the per-item impacts come from 500 replications per cell, with delta-method intervals and, for comparison, intervals from 300 draws of the parameters. The rates at the sum-score cut come from another 500 replications per cell, in which every estimate, SE and classification rule was computed by the package’s own code. The first two parts used the development version of the same computations, which gives the same results as the package to four decimals on a test dataset. A coverage of .95 has a Monte Carlo SE of .007 with 1000 and .010 with 500 replications. No replication failed.


6.5.2 Which classification rule the rates describe
A person’s classification depends only on their raw score, so the classification rule is the set of raw scores at or above the cut, per group and strategy. On the \(\theta\) scale it is read off a WLE table. The rates of the rule in the population make a poor target. Where a population WLE lies within 0.01 logits of the cut, the estimated table puts that raw score on the other side of the cut in about half the samples, and the estimated rates jump with it. Measured against the population rule’s rates, the \(\theta\)-scale rates then covered as little as .636 (median .764), against a lowest coverage of .926 where every WLE was more than 0.05 from the cut. Parameter draws do not help, since that target is a step function of the parameters.
RMdifImpact() therefore takes the rule from the fit and holds it fixed. The target is the rates of that rule under the true model, which are the rates the user’s own classification has. These change smoothly with the parameters, and the delta method applies. The fitted \(\theta\) rule equalled the population rule in 44 to 100% of samples, depending on the cell, so the rule is reported with the rates, as the lowest raw score classified at or above the cut per group and strategy.


6.5.3 Coverage
With the rule held fixed, the rates are close to nominal on both scales, in the sample and projected (Figure 6.8). On the \(\theta\) scale, 29 of 504 rates in the sample (one per group, strategy, cell and kind of rate) cover .931 or less (two Monte Carlo SEs below .95), against about 12 expected by chance. On the sum-score scale the rates covered .916 to .976 (.950) in the sample and .920 to .976 (.948) projected. Keep and split give the same rates whenever their rules agree, so many rows are duplicates, and the excess of low rows is a slight undercoverage and no more. The delta-method SE agrees with the SD of the parameter draws (ratio 0.96 to 1.03, median 1.002), so the draws are not needed. The projected impact and its size in SE units are calibrated as well.








Figure 6.8: Study 3. Coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals (left) and SE ratio, the mean SE divided by the SD of the error (right). Each small point is one quantity in one cell (for the rates, one rate for one group and strategy), jittered vertically. The diamond is the median. Grey band: .95 ± two Monte Carlo SEs for the number of replications. Rates use delta-method intervals for the rates of the fitted rule. The keep − split rows are per cell, over the replications where the two fitted rules differ (cells with at least 100 such replications). Values in Table 6.8.





Keep − split. The difference is zero, with an SE of zero, whenever the two strategies give the same rule, which inflates its coverage. Over the replications where the rules differ, the pooled coverage in the sample is .956 on the \(\theta\) scale and .954 on the sum-score scale. Per cell it is less even. On the \(\theta\) scale, 24 of 354 rows (sample and projected) with at least 100 such replications cover less than .93, the lowest .840. On the sum-score scale the lowest is .924. When the rules differ by one raw score, the difference is the share of persons with that score, and its error is skewed. This interval is the least accurate of the outputs.
Per-item impact. The per-item estimate is close to proportional to \(\widehat{\text{DIF}}_j\), so its SE is the slope of that line times the SE of the shift, \(|\widehat{\text{impact}}_j / \widehat{\text{DIF}}_j| \times
SE(\widehat{\text{DIF}}_j)\), with the SE from the CML covariance matrix. It covers .912 to .982 (.948). The lowest value is for an item in the cell with two central items, DIF = 0.8 and 800/200. The SE from the local gradient of the split model, \(|\partial \Delta_\text{split} / \partial\, \text{DIF}_j| \times
SE(\widehat{\text{DIF}}_j)\), covered only .862 to .944 (.901), since making item \(j\) common moves \(\Delta\) by more than the local gradient predicts.


6.5.4 Signed rates
Under keep, the focal group gets more false negatives and fewer false positives at the \(\theta\) cut than under split (Figure 6.9). With ten items the reference group shows the reverse, and with five items its rates hardly change. The values are the rates of the fitted rule under the true model, averaged over replications. With five items, one central DIF item of 0.8 raises the focal false-negative rate from .061 to .096 and lowers the false-positive rate from .097 to .052. With ten items and one DIF item, the focal rates change by at most 1.4 percentage points. The rates also depend on where the cut falls between the WLE values of neighbouring raw scores. With five four-category items there are only 16 raw scores, and in the example above the split rule classifies .344 of the focal group at or above the cut against a true share of .309 (keep .265).
On the sum-score scale, the reference group’s rule is the same under keep and split, and the focal group’s rule changes when equating moves a raw score across the cut. With one DIF item of 0.8, the focal rule differed between keep and split in 71 to 95% of samples. With two items in the same direction it differed in 92 to 99% at DIF = 0.5 and in all samples at DIF = 0.8. With one item of 0.5 it differed in 2 to 14%, and with two items in opposite directions, whose effects on the raw score largely cancel, in at most 3.6%. For two central items of 0.8 at 500/500, the focal false-negative rate is .086 under keep and .056 under split.








Figure 6.9: Study 3. False-negative and false-positive rates at θ = 1 by WLE, under keep and split, as shares of each group. 500/500, focal mean 0.5. True shares at or above the cut: reference .159, focal .309. Each value is the mean over replications of the fitted rule’s rates under the true model. Values in Table 6.9.
